digest.intro: War economics, cellular time travel, and the machines that are quietly eating everything.

items.title: US Warns Gulf States of a 'Short and Intense' Iran Strike After November 3
items.blurb: Washington has privately warned Gulf Arab states to prepare for a post-midterm military campaign against Iran's infrastructure and nuclear facilities — a Patriot battery is already en route to Israel, a second carrier strike group arrives next month, and Brent is back above $115 after Houthi missiles targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia. Trump hasn't formally decided, but his public language ('maybe we'll do another little Epic Fury') and the Pentagon's release of a $47.1B war cost estimate suggest the decision architecture is being built. The signals are coherent enough that the Gulf states are taking them seriously.

items.title: Israel's Election: No Majority, Highest Turnout Since 1999
items.blurb: Israel's first election since October 7 ended with 77.7% turnout — the highest since 1999 — and no one close to a governing majority: Netanyahu's bloc sits around 54 seats, Eisenkot's at 49, with Palestinian parties winning 17 seats in their strongest performance ever. Both leading candidates have ruled out governing with those Palestinian parties, meaning neither can reach 61. The result lands at the worst possible moment for anyone trying to coordinate a coherent regional posture ahead of a possible Iran operation.

items.title: The Grid: A Factory-Scale Robot That Builds PCBs On Demand in Massachusetts
items.blurb: CircuitHub's Grid uses magnetically levitating movers to carry each board on its own unique route through solder paste printing, component placement, reflow, and inspection — no changeovers, no per-design setup, no minimum order. They've been running it quietly for five years and are now making it public; the pitch is that it handles high-mix, low-volume work (ten of this, a hundred of that, new revision next week) faster than Shenzhen at competitive cost. The physical-digital fabrication loop closing in hardware, at small-batch scale, in the US.

items.title: CNC Stone Carving — Carmelite Gothic
items.blurb: Someone is using CNC machining to reproduce Gothic cathedral stonework with the obsessive precision that medieval masons applied by hand over decades. It's the rare case where digital fabrication isn't flattening a craft but restoring access to one that was effectively lost — the kind of unreasonably deep commitment to a material and a tradition that makes everything else feel approximate.

items.title: Tom Hegen's 'The Mineral Age': Aerial Photography of the Green Transition's Extraction Cost
items.blurb: German photographer Tom Hegen spent six years flying over the sites that will supply the 6.5 billion tons of cobalt, copper, lithium, and nickel the world needs to mine before 2050 — and the resulting 247-image book makes the systemic violence legible as pure color and geometry: candy-pink lithium evaporation ponds in the Atacama, ochre nickel pits butting against Indonesian rainforest. Systems made visible from altitude is a particular kind of argument, and Hegen makes it without editorializing.

items.title: The October Inflection Point for Vibe Game Development
items.blurb: Willison's claim is specific: Claude Opus 5.5 crossed a threshold this month where telling it to 'make it a LOT more fun' actually worked — not aesthetically but structurally, producing genuine gameplay loops with proper challenge curves. He built four games he actually enjoyed playing, and reports that multiple people at Foo Camp last weekend had independently hit the same realization. The new bottleneck, he says, isn't execution — it's concept.

items.title: Delaware Proposes Letting AI Agents Run Entire Companies — With Owners Off the Hook
items.blurb: Delaware's draft 'Artificial Intelligence Company' bill would create a new corporate entity class operated entirely by AI agents, with human owners shielded from liability for the AI's decisions — any lawful purpose except banking. House Oversight chair James Comer is now demanding documents and signaling a federal law to cap state AI regulatory authority, framing it as a liability-laundering vehicle. The structure being proposed here is genuinely novel: not AI as tool inside a company, but AI as the legally operative entity of the company.

items.title: The 1607 Bristol Channel Flood and the Meaning-Making Machine of Early Print
items.blurb: When a storm surge killed 2,000 people and inundated 518 square kilometers around the Bristol Channel in January 1607, London's presses immediately converted the disaster into divine judgment — pamphleteer William Jones had God's interpretation in print before the floodwaters receded. Erik Crnkovich's essay tracks how the Little Ice Age's chronic weather extremes and the booming early-modern news industry co-evolved to manufacture a genre: the providential disaster narrative, which framed every earthquake, flood, and apparition as a moral weathervane. It's a portrait of a society doing in broadsheets exactly what we do in social media — collapsing the incomprehensible into shared meaning at speed.

items.title: The Amarna Letters: Bronze Age Rulers' Petty Disputes and Pleas for Gold
items.blurb: The Amarna Letters are 3,400-year-old clay tablets — diplomatic correspondence between Egyptian pharaohs and the rulers of Babylon, Assyria, and the Hittites — and they read like a group chat of thin-skinned leaders haggling over gold shipments and complaining about protocol slights. Aeon Video tends to be tightly produced and genuinely educational; this one earns its place on a day when you're watching two nuclear-adjacent powers eye each other across the Persian Gulf.

facts.fact: The 1607 Bristol Channel flood killed 2,000 people and inundated 518 square kilometers — and London pamphleteers had theological explanations in print almost immediately, treating the disaster as divine judgment.

Israel's October 2026 election saw 77.7% voter turnout — the highest since 1999 — yet Palestinian parties, despite winning their strongest-ever 17 Knesset seats, were ruled out as coalition partners by both leading candidates.

Delaware's proposed 'Artificial Intelligence Company' bill would allow AI agents to legally operate entire businesses in any industry except banking, with human owners shielded from liability for the AI's decisions.

The global green transition is projected to require mining 6.5 billion tons of cobalt, copper, lithium, nickel, and other materials before 2050 — most of it concentrated in a handful of countries already most exposed to climate impacts.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A first-person essay-film structured as letters from a wandering cameraman — it's less a documentary than a meditation on how memory, image, and ritual encode culture, traveling from Tokyo's vending-machine shrines to Guinea-Bissau's post-revolutionary ceremonies. Obsessive systems-thinking disguised as travelogue; the invisible forces you love are its entire subject.

art_picks.title: Hubris
art_picks.creator: Oren Ambarchi
art_picks.why: A single 39-minute piece built entirely from guitar, bass, and drums locked into interlocking rhythmic systems that gradually drift and compound — it's generative logic disguised as rock music, the kind of obsessive narrow-focus craft that reveals depth the longer you stay inside it.

art_picks.title: Haegue Yang: Through
art_picks.creator: Haegue Yang
art_picks.why: Yang's kinetic, material sculptures — Venetian blind slats, bells, sensor-driven light — function as physical systems that encode cultural memory and ritual through industrial materials. The DIA Beacon space turns her work into environment; the physical-digital edge you build in lives inside the formal logic she's worked out over decades.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, Manhattan
events.why: fMRI brain scans fed to a neural net that generates hallucinatory visual reconstructions, spread across freestanding screens in MoMA's garden and activated in real time by visitor gaze and cancer-cell mutation data — it's literally a system that thinks alongside you, and it closes in a month.

events.name: EJ Hauser: Sun Water Sky
events.venue: Derek Eller Gallery, 38 Walker Street, Manhattan
events.why: Hauser's paintings sit at the edge of landscape and pure mark-making — intuitive systems of color that read simultaneously as atmosphere and abstraction, the kind of expressive surface with deep structural logic underneath that tends to make painters want to go back to the studio.

events.name: Oren Ambarchi Solo — Kou Records at Blank Forms
events.venue: Blank Forms, 151 Lafayette Street, 6th floor, Manhattan
events.why: Ambarchi flying in from Berlin for a rare solo set at one of the city's best small listening spaces — extended guitar with a new record just out, and the room holds the obsessive craft without diluting it.

events.name: Oren Ambarchi / Andrew Cyrille / Cyro Baptista — First-Ever Trio
events.venue: Blank Forms, 151 Lafayette Street, 6th floor, Manhattan
events.why: Night two of Ambarchi's residency pairs him with jazz percussion legend Andrew Cyrille and Brazilian percussionist/vocalist Cyro Baptista for a completely improvised trio that has never played together before — three distinct musical systems colliding live.

events.name: Oliver Bak — Solo Exhibition
events.venue: Sprüth Magers New York, 22 East 80th Street
events.why: The young Danish painter's New York debut at Sprüth Magers — his oil-and-wax figures emerge from and dissolve back into their backgrounds, monochromatic veils over bodies and blossoms that blur the boundary between presence and environment; a rare gallery show with real pictorial ambition.
